lessonTitle: Acute Kidney Injury: Recognition, Causes and Emergency Management

blocks.text: A 74-year-old woman on ramipril, furosemide and regular ibuprofen has had three days of diarrhoea. Her usual creatinine is 70 µmol/L; today it is 168 µmol/L and her bladder scan is empty. Which part of the kidney's plumbing has failed, and what must you do in the next hour?

blocks.markdown: The kidney filters blood at the glomerulus, processes the filtrate along the tubule, and drains urine through the collecting system, ureters, bladder and urethra. **Acute kidney injury (AKI)** is a sudden fall in filtration. Anything that starves the glomerulus of blood (**prerenal**), damages the kidney tissue itself (**intrinsic** or **renal**), or blocks the outflow of urine (**postrenal**) can cause it. Sorting a patient into one of these three groups is the first step because the treatments are completely different: fluid, stopping a toxin or immune attack, or relieving an obstruction.

blocks.title: Acute kidney injury (KDIGO/NICE style definition)
blocks.text: AKI is present if ANY of: a rise in serum creatinine of 26 µmol/L or more within 48 hours; a rise to 1.5 times the baseline or more within 7 days; or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h for more than 6 consecutive hours. Creatinine is only a lagging marker: it rises hours to days after filtration falls.

blocks.caption: Oliguria criterion for AKI: below 0.5 mL/kg/h for more than 6 hours.

blocks.title: Staging AKI from creatinine
blocks.prompt: A man's baseline creatinine is 80 µmol/L. On admission with sepsis it is 176 µmol/L. Is this AKI and what stage (stage 1: 1.5 to 1.9 times baseline; stage 2: 2.0 to 2.9 times; stage 3: 3.0 times or more, or creatinine above 354 µmol/L, or need for renal replacement)?

steps.text: Calculate the ratio of current to baseline creatinine.
A ratio of at least 1.5 within 7 days meets the AKI definition.
A ratio of 2.2 lies between 2.0 and 2.9, so this is stage 2. The absolute value (176) is below 354 so the stage 3 absolute criterion is not met.

rows: Hypovolaemia (bleeding, vomiting, diarrhoea), sepsis, heart failure, ACE inhibitor/ARB plus NSAID
Bland dipstick; concentrated urine, low urine sodium; urea rises more than creatinine; improves with fluid
Damage to tubules, glomeruli, interstitium or vessels
Acute tubular necrosis (prolonged ischaemia or toxins such as aminoglycosides, contrast), glomerulonephritis, acute interstitial nephritis
ATN: muddy brown granular casts; glomerulonephritis: blood, protein, red cell casts; interstitial nephritis: white cells, drug history
Prostatic enlargement, bladder or pelvic malignancy, stones, blocked catheter
Palpable or scanned bladder, hydronephrosis on ultrasound; may have fluctuating urine volumes
blocks.caption: The three categories of AKI.

blocks.markdown: **Interpreting the first blood and urine tests in an oliguric patient.** Urea and creatinine both rise as filtration falls. In prerenal states the tubule reabsorbs urea avidly with water and sodium, so **urea rises disproportionately to creatinine**; a gastrointestinal bleed, which adds a protein (urea) load from digested blood, exaggerates this. **Potassium** is excreted mainly by the distal nephron, so oliguria leads to hyperkalaemia, worsened by acidosis, tissue breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) and drugs such as ACE inhibitors, spironolactone and trimethoprim. **Urinalysis** is cheap and informative: a bland dipstick favours prerenal causes; blood and protein suggest glomerular disease; leucocytes and nitrite suggest infection; granular casts suggest ATN. Always examine for a distended bladder and arrange a bladder scan or catheter, and arrange renal tract ultrasound if the cause is unclear or obstruction is possible.

blocks.title: Is this oliguria?
blocks.prompt: A 90 kg man is catheterised after major surgery. Over the next 6 hours the bag collects 150 mL. Does he meet the urine-output criterion for AKI?

steps.text: Compare with the threshold of 0.5 mL/kg/h sustained for more than 6 hours. 0.28 is well below it, so the criterion is met.
Next questions: is the catheter blocked or kinked, is he hypovolaemic, are his drugs nephrotoxic? Check potassium and creatinine now rather than waiting.

blocks.answer: 0.28 mL/kg/h: oliguria meeting AKI criteria; investigate for prerenal, intrinsic and obstructive causes.

items: Emergency treatment of hyperkalaemia (K+ 6.5 mmol/L or above, or any ECG change): obtain an ECG and monitor the rhythm.

Protect the heart first: IV calcium: 30 mL of 10% calcium gluconate (or 10 mL of 10% calcium chloride) over 5 to 10 minutes with continuous ECG monitoring, repeated if ECG changes persist. Check doses and the preferred preparation against current UK Kidney Association, Resuscitation Council UK, BNF and local guidance. It stabilises the myocardial membrane but does not lower potassium.

Shift potassium into cells: short-acting insulin with glucose (teaching example: 10 units insulin in 25 g glucose) and nebulised salbutamol. Check capillary glucose afterwards for hypoglycaemia. Insulin and salbutamol doses are teaching examples only: check against current UK Kidney Association, BNF and local guidance.
Remove potassium from the body: treat the cause, stop potassium-raising drugs, consider a potassium binder or loop diuretic if the patient is not hypovolaemic, and use dialysis if refractory.

Indications for urgent renal replacement therapy: refractory hyperkalaemia, severe metabolic acidosis, fluid overload with pulmonary oedema unresponsive to diuretics, uraemic complications (pericarditis, encephalopathy), and certain dialysable toxins.

blocks.title: Do not forget the obstruction
blocks.text: A normal-looking urine volume does not exclude obstruction, and relieving a postrenal block (by catheter or nephrostomy) is the most rapidly reversible treatment in all of AKI. Always ask: could this be obstructed?

blocks.title: Management bundle
blocks.text: Stage the AKI, look for and treat the cause (sepsis, hypovolaemia, obstruction), stop or adjust nephrotoxic and renally cleared drugs, check potassium and ECG, assess fluid status and aim for euvolaemia, monitor urine output, and know when to escalate to nephrology or dialysis.

points: AKI is defined by a rapid creatinine rise or low urine output and is staged by the size of the rise.
Classify AKI as prerenal, intrinsic or postrenal; always exclude obstruction and review drugs.
Urea, creatinine, potassium and urinalysis help distinguish the categories and identify life-threatening complications.
Hyperkalaemia with ECG change: calcium to protect the heart, insulin-glucose and salbutamol to shift potassium, then removal.
Urgent dialysis is for refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, overload, uraemic complications and some toxins.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has had five days of vomiting and poor oral intake. BP is 88/50 mmHg, he is tachycardic with dry mucous membranes, and urinalysis is bland. Creatinine has doubled from baseline. Which category of AKI is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: hypovolaemia with a bland urine points to reduced perfusion of structurally intact kidneys.
distractorRationale.b: Glomerular disease would give blood and protein on dipstick, not a bland sediment.
distractorRationale.c: Obstruction would be suggested by a palpable bladder or hydronephrosis, which are not described.
distractorRationale.d: Interstitial nephritis typically follows a drug exposure and shows white cells in the urine.

questions.explanation: The history of volume loss, hypotension and tachycardia together with a bland urinalysis shows the kidneys are underperfused but not structurally damaged. Prompt fluid resuscitation usually reverses this form of AKI.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old man with long-standing difficulty passing urine has had no urine for 10 hours. He has suprapubic discomfort and a palpable, dull bladder. What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Insert a urinary catheter and measure the residual volume

questions.correctOptionText: Insert a urinary catheter and measure the residual volume

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is postrenal obstruction and catheterisation relieves it.
distractorRationale.b: A large fluid load in an obstructed, possibly volume-replete patient risks overload and does not relieve the block.
distractorRationale.c: Dialysis is not the first step when a rapidly reversible obstruction can be drained.
distractorRationale.d: Diuretics do not unblock the outflow and can worsen hypovolaemia.

questions.explanation: The history of prostatic symptoms with anuria and a dull palpable bladder indicates postrenal obstruction. Catheter drainage is simple, safe and the definitive early treatment, and the volume drained and subsequent urine output guide further care, including watching for post-obstructive diuresis.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman had a ruptured appendix, was hypotensive for several hours before surgery, and remains oliguric despite adequate fluid resuscitation. Urine microscopy shows many muddy brown granular casts. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Prerenal azotaemia that will correct with more fluid

distractorRationale.a: Correct: prolonged hypoperfusion plus failure to respond to fluid and granular casts indicate ischaemic ATN.
distractorRationale.b: Prerenal AKI would respond to fluid and show a bland sediment.
distractorRationale.c: Glomerulonephritis would show red cell casts and haematuria.
distractorRationale.d: Obstruction is not suggested and does not produce granular casts.

questions.explanation: Granular (muddy brown) casts are sloughed tubular epithelial cells and are characteristic of ATN. The lack of response to restored perfusion shows the tubular damage has already occurred, so management is supportive while the tubule regenerates.

questions.stem: A patient with AKI has serum potassium 7.0 mmol/L, peaked T waves and a widened QRS on the ECG. Which treatment should be given first?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: calcium stabilises the cardiac membrane against arrhythmia within minutes.
distractorRationale.b: Salbutamol shifts potassium but takes longer and does not protect the myocardium directly.
distractorRationale.c: Binders act slowly over hours and are not emergency cardioprotection.
distractorRationale.d: Insulin-glucose lowers potassium but does not immediately protect the heart, so it follows calcium.

questions.explanation: With ECG changes the immediate threat is arrhythmia, so membrane stabilisation with IV calcium is given first. It does not reduce the potassium concentration, so insulin-glucose and salbutamol must follow to shift potassium into cells, and removal measures treat the underlying excess.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man presents with haematemesis. Blood results show urea 32 mmol/L, creatinine 130 µmol/L (baseline 100 µmol/L). Which interpretation best explains the disproportionate urea rise?

options.text: Reduced renal perfusion plus absorbed protein load from digested blood

questions.correctOptionText: Reduced renal perfusion plus absorbed protein load from digested blood

distractorRationale.a: Correct: hypovolaemia increases urea reabsorption and blood in the gut is digested to urea.
distractorRationale.b: Glomerulonephritis would show urinary blood and protein, not a selective urea rise.
distractorRationale.c: Rhabdomyolysis raises creatinine and potassium and causes dark urine rather than a disproportionate urea rise.
distractorRationale.d: Obstruction raises both urea and creatinine and does not explain the bleed.

questions.explanation: Urea is reabsorbed in the tubule along with water when perfusion is low, and the absorbed products of digested blood add to the urea load. Creatinine is produced by muscle at a steady rate and so rises proportionally less.

questions.stem: A 80 kg patient on the ward is catheterised and produces 240 mL of urine over 12 hours. Calculate the average urine output in mL/kg/h (unit: mL/kg/h).
questions.explanation: Urine output per kilogram per hour is 240 / (80 x 12) = 0.25 mL/kg/h. This is below the 0.5 mL/kg/h threshold sustained over more than 6 hours, so he meets the urine-output criterion for AKI and needs assessment for cause.

questions.stem: A woman's baseline creatinine is 60 µmol/L. After a course of antibiotics her creatinine is 190 µmol/L. By what factor has the creatinine risen relative to baseline (unit: fold, i.e. ratio)? Give your answer to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The ratio is 190 / 60 = 3.17. A rise to 3.0 times baseline or more is stage 3 AKI, so this patient needs urgent assessment for the cause and consideration of the need for renal replacement.

questions.stem: List and explain the indications for urgent renal replacement therapy (dialysis) in a patient with AKI.
markingGuide: Hyperkalaemia refractory to medical treatment or with persisting ECG change
Severe or worsening metabolic acidosis not responding to treatment
Fluid overload or pulmonary oedema unresponsive to diuretics
Uraemic complications such as pericarditis or encephalopathy
Poisoning with a dialysable toxin or drug
Explains that these are failures of the kidney to excrete potassium, acid, water and urea, and dialysis substitutes for those functions
questions.explanation: Renal replacement is indicated when the kidney's missing functions threaten life and medical therapy is failing or inadequate. The indications are therefore refractory hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis, diuretic-resistant overload, uraemic complications and certain dialysable toxins, and each reflects a failure to excrete a specific substance.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with sepsis has oliguria and rising creatinine. Describe how you would use urinalysis, urine biochemistry and response to fluids to distinguish prerenal AKI from acute tubular necrosis.
markingGuide: Prerenal: bland dipstick and sediment; ATN: granular or muddy brown casts
Prerenal: low urine sodium and concentrated urine as the tubule retains sodium and water
ATN: higher urine sodium and dilute urine because tubular function is lost
Prerenal improves after restoration of volume and perfusion; ATN does not respond promptly
Interprets urine sodium cautiously, since diuretics confound it
Also excludes obstruction with bladder scan or ultrasound
questions.explanation: In prerenal AKI the tubules are working, so they conserve sodium and water and the urine is concentrated with a bland sediment, and function improves when perfusion is restored. In ATN the tubular cells are damaged, so sodium is not retained, the urine is dilute with granular casts, and there is no prompt recovery; diuretics can confuse urine sodium, so the whole picture is used.

questions.stem: True or false: a serum creatinine within the laboratory reference range, measured one hour after an acute fall in glomerular filtration, excludes significant AKI.
questions.explanation: Creatinine accumulates gradually after filtration falls, so it can remain normal for hours to days despite a large drop in filtration. This is why urine output and the clinical context matter as well as the creatinine, and why creatinine is a lagging marker.
